idiom_name: defined?(@derived) guard plus remove_instance_variable as invalidation
implementation_notes: The community memoization idiom carries the pattern: `@derived = compute unless defined?(@derived)` recomputes only when the instance variable is absent, and invalidation removes the variable with remove_instance_variable (which also returns the old value), so the flag is the variable's existence rather than a bool. This is the correct form for values that may legitimately be nil or false, where `@derived ||= compute` would recompute on every read. Ruby's attribute writers do not intercept assignment, so the invalidation call must live in a method the class owns; attr_accessor on the primary data bypasses the pattern entirely.
pitfalls: `||=` treats false and nil as 'not cached', so a legitimate nil/false result recomputes on every read - use defined? for the guard.
attr_writer/attr_accessor on the primary data bypasses invalidation completely; hide writers behind methods that also drop the cache.
Frozen objects cannot memoise: writing an instance variable on a frozen object raises FrozenError (Ractor-shareable objects are frozen), so lazy caches must be built before freezing.
remove_instance_variable is not atomic with the read: two threads can both rebuild, and MRI's GVL is released during blocking work, so shared instances need a Mutex.

variants.name: Mutex-synchronized recomputation
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby threads share memory, and the GVL does not make a multi-step check-and-rebuild atomic, so a shared instance wraps the recomputation in a Thread::Mutex#synchronize block and re-checks the guard inside the lock - the same double-checked shape as in other languages, with the cache published before the accessor returns. The mutex is the stdlib primitive for coordinating access to shared data across threads; the guard keeps repeated reads lock-free only if reads of an already-computed value avoid the mutex, which means accepting that the published value is effectively immutable. For true parallelism without a shared heap, Ractors (with frozen/shareable state) or processes are the alternative.
pitfalls: Mutex#synchronize is reentrant-safe only per instance as documented (it raises ThreadError on recursive lock attempts by the same thread); a rebuild that calls back into the same object deadlocks or raises.
The mutex must not be re-created per call, and the cached value must not be replaced by a fresh mutex during Marshal.load or dup - the lock has to be re-established explicitly.
Holding the mutex during a long recomputation serialises all readers; publish an immutable value and let subsequent reads skip the lock if that matters.
Mutual exclusion fixes visibility only inside synchronize: a fast path that reads @world without the lock can see a stale value, so it must read after the lock was last released or not at all.
